title: Why Do People Insist on Holding Far Too Many Team Meetings
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Draws a sharp line between outputs (tangible activity like meetings, deliverables, presentations) and outcomes (the actual results those activities are meant to produce), arguing organizations default to rewarding the former because it's easier to observe and control. Traces how output-rewarding cultures cause meeting proliferation, since meetings become the visible symbol of productivity even when they don't move outcomes. The prescribed fix is defining outcomes first, then working backward to determine which outputs actually serve them, replacing many meetings with alternatives like written briefs, dashboards, and problem statements.
points: Organizations default to rewarding outputs over outcomes because activity is easier to observe and control than actual results.
Meeting-heavy cultures form specifically because meetings function as a visible, countable symbol of productivity, regardless of whether they move outcomes.

The fix is to define measurable outcomes first, then align outputs (including whether meetings are even necessary) to serve them, replacing many meetings with briefs, dashboards, or problem statements.
quotes: Outputs are the tangible activities and deliverables a team produces, such as meetings held, calls made, features launched, and presentations delivered.
When leaders mistake outputs for success, teams can appear productive without actually advancing strategic goals.
A meeting-heavy culture develops because outputs are easier to observe and control than outcomes. It feels safer to count tasks than to evaluate whether real change has occurred.
Good leaders reverse this pattern by defining clear, measurable outcomes first and then aligning outputs to support them.
Meetings should exist only if they directly advance a defined outcome (like a decision or strategy implementation).
Progress compounds when teams spend less time talking about work and more time improving results.
